analysis.one_liner: Bans EPA climate rules, voids coal plant and interstate air pollution rules, and blocks new coal mining regulations.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 233-175 on September 21, 2012, but the Senate referred it to committee and never voted, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stripped the EPA of nearly all authority to regulate greenhouse gases for climate purposes, repealing its finding that carbon emissions endanger public health, and voided two major air pollution rules for coal-fired power plants: the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule and the proposed mercury and air toxics standards. It also barred the Interior Department from issuing any new coal mining rules through 2013 that would reduce the amount of coal available for mining, and it restricted the EPA's power to overrule state water quality decisions. A final title singled out the coal-fired Navajo Generating Station in Arizona for protection from visibility rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies, coal- and oil-fired electric utilities, and owners of the Navajo Generating Station. Utilities would get the interstate smog rule thrown out, the mercury and air toxics rule erased and replaced on a delayed schedule, and at least five years of extra compliance time. Mining companies would be shielded from any Interior Department rule through 2013 that cuts coal available for mining or affects coal jobs. States would gain final say over coal ash disposal permits and most water quality standards, with the EPA barred from concurrent enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal mining companies and coal-fired power utilities

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Interior Secretary through December 31, 2013 from issuing any mining rule that would adversely impact coal mine employment, reduce coal available for domestic consumption or export, or designate any area unsuitable for surface mining.

Prohibits the EPA from promulgating any regulation of greenhouse gas emissions to address climate change, removes greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act's definition of an air pollutant, and repeals and voids the endangerment finding, the greenhouse gas reporting rule, and the permitting rules that applied the Clean Air Act to carbon emissions.

Nullifies the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule (replacing it with the older, weaker Clean Air Interstate Rule) and throws out the proposed mercury and air toxics standards for coal- and oil-fired power plants, requiring replacement rules no earlier than a year after a new cumulative-impact study and compliance no earlier than five years after those rules take effect.

Bans the EPA from granting or honoring California's waiver for greenhouse gas vehicle standards for model year 2017 and later, keeping a single federal vehicle standard, while exempting the existing federal vehicle greenhouse gas rules from the bill's ban.

Protects the coal-fired Navajo Generating Station and coal mines on Navajo and Hopi lands in northern Arizona from any federal visibility rule that would cut jobs, coal revenue tied to Indian water rights settlements, or coal deliveries for water and power.

analysis.who_pays: If it had become law, the cost would have fallen on people who live downwind of coal plants and near mines and coal ash dumps: more soot, ozone, mercury, and other pollutants, and unchecked greenhouse gas emissions. Communities would have lost federal backup when state water quality or coal ash programs fall short, and the EPA would have been barred from setting ozone and soot standards using data not made public, or from acting on new standards until three years after a cumulative study finished in 2013.
analysis.who_pays_short: People near coal plants, mines, and ash dumps

drawbacks.text: Supporters' core argument was that stacked EPA rules threatened electricity prices, jobs in coal regions, and grid reliability; the bill itself directed a new interagency committee to measure the combined impact of EPA rules on electricity and fuel prices, employment, and low-income communities before some rules could proceed.

The bill did contain regulation of its own: it required state coal ash permit programs with independent engineer certifications of dam stability, annual impoundment inspections, groundwater monitoring, and financial assurance, rather than leaving coal ash entirely unregulated.

Delaying and rewriting the mercury and air toxics standards, and requiring the EPA to base national air standards on actual monitored data and cost and feasibility considerations, would postpone health protections for people exposed to power plant pollution and set weaker baselines for new rules.

Blocking California's vehicle emissions waiver and barring the Transportation Secretary from consulting the EPA or California officials except for basic facts would have removed the stricter state vehicle standards that California and other states had adopted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine uncertainties the bill raised about cumulative regulatory costs were addressed mainly by ordering studies, while the bill's operative provisions repealed or froze existing health and environmental protections. The coal ash title added real minimum requirements, but the overall design traded enforceable federal standards for state discretion and long delays that fell hardest on people living near polluting facilities. The climate provisions were categorical: no EPA climate regulation at all, under any administration, rather than a recalibrated one.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 233-175 near the end of the 2012 session, but the Senate referred it to its environment committee on November 13, 2012 and never voted on it, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported 26-16 and reported it on September 13, 2012.

The House debated the bill under a rule on September 20-21, 2012, adopting a substitute amendment and several amendments while rejecting Democratic amendments offered by Reps. Markey, Waxman, DeFazio, and Jackson Lee.
A motion by Rep. Lois Capps to recommit the bill with instructions protecting the 2017-2025 vehicle fuel efficiency rule failed 173-233, with every Republican voting no.
The House passed the bill on final passage 233-175: 214 of 239 voting Republicans and 19 of 190 voting Democrats in favor.
The Senate received the bill on November 13, 2012 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where no further action occurred before the Congress ended January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained the rollbacks it promised: the EPA's greenhouse gas, interstate transport, mercury, and coal mining rules remained in effect, so communities near coal plants and mines kept the protections the bill would have stripped. Coal mining and utility companies, which had backed the bill, lost their chance at those changes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who breathe air near coal plants

industries.note: The bill barred the Interior Department from any 2013 mining rule that would cut coal available for mining, affect coal jobs, or designate land unsuitable for mining, blocking new stream and land protections. Their gain comes at the cost of pollution controls on mining communities downstream.

The bill voided the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule and the proposed mercury and air toxics standards, delayed replacement rules and set five-year minimum compliance times, and kept the older, weaker Clean Air Interstate Rule in place. Utilities avoided retrofit costs while people downwind absorbed more pollution.

industries.industry: Coal ash disposal (utilities and state permit programs)
industries.note: The bill's coal ash title created state permit programs with engineering certifications, inspections, and groundwater monitoring, but barred federal concurrent enforcement and kept coal ash out of hazardous waste regulation. It locked in state-level control as the permanent channel for regulating coal combustion waste, with federal backup only if a state opted out or failed.

The bill exempted the existing federal vehicle greenhouse gas and fuel economy rules from its ban, preserving one national standard automakers preferred, but banned California's stricter waiver for 2017 and later model years, relieving automakers of having to meet the tightest state requirements.

industries.industry: Navajo Generating Station owners and tribal coal operations in northern Arizona
industries.note: A dedicated title barred any federal visibility rule that would cost jobs at the plant or reduce coal revenue on Navajo and Hopi lands tied to Indian water rights settlements. It protected regional coal employment and revenue while keeping the plant's haze and pollution contribution in place.
